content.title: China and Russia could launch a two-front war against the West. Europe must be prepared for all scenarios
content.lead: Moscow could support Beijing in an attack on Taiwan – and simultaneously attack NATO. The authoritarian regimes are already cooperating. Three factors could accelerate an escalation.
content.author: Lukas Mäder, Georg Häsler

image.author: Kevin Frayer / Getty
image.caption: If China attacks Taiwan, Russia could help with its own military action: Sailors of the Chinese Navy in Qingdao in April 2024.

content.text: In the Red Sea, a Chinese warship aimed its laser at a German reconnaissance aircraft. Berlin protested, Beijing denied it. In the Baltic Sea, a submarine cable snapped. Authorities suspect sabotage. The Chinese ship «Yi Peng 3» is alleged to have deliberately dragged its anchor along the seabed. There is no clear evidence, but plenty of suspicion.

China is interfering, not only on the other side of the Eurasian landmass, but also in Europe and the Middle East. Its autocratic attack on Western democracies is not limited to territorial claims in its neighborhood, but is developing into a global conflict.

In early July, China's foreign minister made it unequivocally clear to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas that Beijing had an interest in Russia winning the war against Ukraine—or at least not losing it. Shortly afterward, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned that Russia and China could jointly attack the West. If Beijing were to launch an invasion of Taiwan, the Kremlin would simultaneously tie up NATO forces in Eastern Europe through escalation.

content.title: The strategic position of the Houthi

content.text: Such a scenario would have been unthinkable just a few years ago. Now its likelihood is increasing. Since the beginning of the war in Ukraine, the Moscow-Beijing axis has been developing into an alliance of two autocracies with imperial ambitions. Their rejection of liberal democratic values ​​serves as a unifying element.

The danger of global escalation is growing. Individual conflicts are merging, and the actors involved are closely intertwined. The Houthi militias in Yemen exemplify this development: they receive support from Iran, which collaborates closely with Russia. China, in turn, provides technological support not only to Iran but also to the Houthi militia itself. The Red Sea is becoming a geopolitical and global economic flashpoint.

Moreover, the Houthis are not only fighting for their dominance in Yemen. With their attacks on cargo ships, they are also significantly disrupting the trade route between Europe and Asia. This is one of the main reasons why the US has been conducting regular airstrikes against positions in South Yemen for months. This has not changed with the change of power in Washington. The Trump administration is continuing what Biden began.

content.text: Washington categorizes the recent operations as Freedom of Navigation Operations (Fronop), which ensure that ships have free passage on the world's oceans. The US justifies its actions in the Red Sea similarly to its military presence in the Indo-Pacific. While the Chinese pinpricks against maritime freedom off its own coast are not coordinated with the Houthi attacks, they are linked due to their similar effects.

The escalation of the past weeks and months in the Middle East is tying up Western political and military resources. Public attention, diplomatic efforts, and American military forces are focused on the Iran-Israel-Yemen triangle. As a result, the war in Ukraine has faded into the background. This development benefits Russia.

content.title: The West is running out of ammunition

content.text: The Kremlin has gradually gained the upper hand in recent months: with intensive drone attacks against civilian targets, including in far western Ukraine, and attempts to tear the Ukrainian army apart. The front line is overextended. Russian troops are attempting a breakthrough at at least three points with their summer offensive.

President Donald Trump's attempts to persuade his counterpart Vladimir Putin to agree to a ceasefire have failed – and have significantly weakened Ukraine. Moreover, the Kremlin has succeeded in internationalizing the war of attrition against the West: North Korea is supplying soldiers, Iran is providing drones, and China is supplying technology and satellite data.

The US, on the other hand, has reduced its military aid in recent months. As early as the beginning of 2024, Congress blocked arms deliveries. Since Trump took office, supplies have been completely halted at times. Despite all the noise from Washington, the issue is less about disciplining Kyiv and more about the deep stockpiles of ammunition and guided missiles.

Whether in Europe or the Middle East, the US is using up the ammunition it actually needs for a credible, conventional deterrent in the Indo-Pacific. At times, the Americans even had to procure artillery shells from Israel so that the Ukrainian army could stem the Russian offensive. Meanwhile, the Ukrainians have reduced their own ammunition consumption.

The situation is similar with regard to protecting the Israeli civilian population against Iranian guided missiles. Both Israel itself and its partners involved in the integrated air defense system in the Middle East appear to have reached the limits of what is possible. According to reliable sources, towards the end of the most recent confrontation, the Israelis used only one missile instead of three to intercept an enemy missile.

The «Twelve Day War» of late June 2025 represents the provisional climax of the Iranian-Israeli conflict. First, the Israelis beheaded Hezbollah in Lebanon, then they fought the Houthis in Yemen, and finally the regime in Tehran directly. Even if the consequences of this brief war cannot yet be fully assessed, Israel, together with the US, succeeded in weakening Iran and the Iranian «axis of resistance,» as well as repelling Tehran's nuclear ambitions.

Washington's attempts to end current wars are geopolitically motivated: The Pacific Ocean lies at the center of the American vision, as a CIA map from March 2025 illustrates. In this depiction, Europe and the Middle East are on the periphery of a new world order. Trump wants to complete what began under President Barack Obama: the shift towards Asia, the «pivot to Asia.» But this will only work if there is peace on the fringes.

content.text: The Americans expect the Chinese People's Liberation Army to be militarily ready to launch an offensive by 2027. Regardless of Beijing's actual intentions, the US plans to concentrate the bulk of its forces in the Pacific by then at the latest. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reaffirmed this general direction at the end of May at the Shangri-La Dialogue, the Asian security conference – including the pivotal year of 2027.

Security experts in the Indo-Pacific do not consider a direct invasion of Taiwan in the coming years to be the most likely scenario. Rather, Beijing is attempting to encircle and pressure the island. Nevertheless, videos of landing exercises and new amphibious systems regularly appear on social media timelines. Therefore, a military surprise attack cannot be entirely ruled out – especially not in coordination with Moscow.

content.title: The «little green men» could appear in the EU

content.text: The increasingly close cooperation between Moscow and Beijing carries enormous potential for escalation. In the event of a military attack on Taiwan, it is in China's interest for Russia to simultaneously instigate an escalation of the conflict with Europe. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently addressed this scenario in an interview with the New York Times .

How this escalation could occur can be seen in Russia's actions in Crimea and eastern Ukraine in 2014. At that time, armed forces appeared there, nicknamed «little green men» because of their uniforms. They were Russian soldiers, but they did not identify themselves as such. They called themselves independence fighters and took control of the territories.

A similar scenario is conceivable in several locations in Europe. The «Narva scenario» is often mentioned: an armed group of alleged insurgents could occupy the town hall in the Estonian city of Narva and declare independence. Narva is located in the far northeast of the NATO member Estonia, directly on the Russian border. Ninety-seven percent of the population speaks Russian as their mother tongue .

content.text: Such a covert Kremlin operation would pose a challenge to Estonia and NATO as a whole, because it would raise the question of a proportionate response. However, the escalation doesn't necessarily have to take place in Narva. «Little green men» could, for example, also appear in the Latvian province near the Russian or Belarusian borders, where many people are Russian-speaking, such as in the railway hub of Rezekne.

The Svalbard archipelago, with the Russian mining town of Barentsburg, would also be a potential target for escalation due to its special status under international law . In Moldova, Russia can already exert influence over the breakaway republic of Transnistria. A covert operation would be conceivable, for example, in the autonomous republic of Gagauzia, which is considered pro-Russian . While Moldova is neither a member of the EU nor NATO, an armed conflict in its immediate vicinity would pose a significant political and military challenge for Europe.

content.title: The Russian threat exists independently of China

content.text: A coordinated escalation across multiple theaters would be in the interest of the authoritarian Moscow-Beijing axis. The US would have to respond to the Chinese attack on Taiwan, but would also be involved on Europe's eastern flank through NATO. The EU would be politically preoccupied with its own affairs and could therefore avoid an additional open conflict with China. The autocratic states' intentions would be fulfilled.

But the focus should not be solely on this extreme scenario, which already borders on a third world war. The geopolitical entanglements of the major powers in the various conflict regions already exist today. The «Narva scenario» should not be understood simply as Russian support for China. The threat from the Kremlin already exists today – regardless of Beijing's plans.

Western security agencies have feared for months that the Kremlin could launch an operation in the coming years to test NATO's cohesion. It would be the logical next step given Russia's escalating confrontation with the West. Sabotage of submarine cables, military provocations, arson attacks, and more aggressive influence operations demonstrate that the Kremlin is increasingly and openly attacking Europe.

Russia has prepared for war. A defeat in Ukraine is not anticipated. Accordingly, the Kremlin's willingness to cooperate with the Chinese regime is likely high. A coordinated attack on Taiwan and a NATO member state is an extreme scenario, but cannot be ruled out. More likely, both autocratic regimes will opportunistically exploit any opportunities that arise to escalate the conflict with the democratic West to their own advantage.

For Europe, this means that it should consider and prepare for extreme scenarios. At the same time, policymakers and security authorities must address those escalation options that pose an immediate threat. Developments on the front lines in Ukraine and the political cohesion of the EU are also geopolitical in nature.
From a European perspective, three factors can significantly accelerate an escalation:

Russian breakthrough in Ukraine: Russia is currently advancing the war in Ukraine with heavy losses. So far, the Ukrainian armed forces have been able to repel the attacks. The Russian troops are advancing only very slowly. However, there is a risk that they will achieve a breakthrough at some point in the coming weeks. Then Moscow could quickly make significant territorial gains and inflict painful losses on the Ukrainians. This would put even more political and military pressure on Kyiv. Europe would likely be confronted with a larger wave of refugees, which could also influence the political climate within the EU.

Conflict with the US: EU-US relations have cooled rapidly since Donald Trump took office in January. The trade dispute is currently simmering. A major escalation within NATO has so far been averted, partly because European member states have made significant promises. However, it is uncertain whether this calm will last. Differences over tariffs or NATO spending could erupt into a larger conflict at any time. This would have serious consequences for Europe, as the continent is technologically and militarily dependent on the US. If this cooperation breaks down, the West would be weakened – much to the delight of autocratic regimes.

Crisis within the EU: Right- and left-wing populist, anti-EU forces have gained ground in several countries in recent years. This puts the EU under fundamental pressure, making it more difficult to pursue a coherent policy. While the geopolitical situation becomes more unpredictable and the threat to the free West increases, the EU is preoccupied with its own internal conflicts. An alliance between left- and right-wing populists in Germany could seriously jeopardize European unity.

content.text: French President Emmanuel Macron is right when he says that France's freedom has not been under such intense pressure since 1945 as it is today. His statement, made to soldiers on the eve of France's national holiday, applies to all of Europe. At stake is the resilience of liberal democracy against the onslaught of the authoritarian Moscow-Beijing axis.

European states face the daunting task of both modernizing their own armed forces and enabling Ukraine to extricate itself from a precarious military situation. This may require acknowledging that Europe is already at war with Russia – or at least in open conflict. True peace demands an internal readiness to defend against an attack on freedom.
